newsitem.title: POLAND: FEATURE - Foreigners prefer ex-communist win in Polish polls.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Foreigners prefer ex-communist win in Polish polls.

text.p: Foreign investors, normally suspicious of the left, seem to prefer Poland's ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) of former communists to stay in power after September 21 parliamentary polls, according to London-based economists.

The SLD, which flies a social-democratic banner, has been running neck and neck with a right-wing alliance grouped around the Solidarity trade union, which, despite its pledges to keep reforms on track, is regarded with suspicion.

As no party is likely to be able to rule alone, analysts said the most desirable coalition partner for the SLD would be the opposition Union for Freedom (UW) party, headed by the author of Poland's reforms liberal Leszek Balcerowicz.
The two parties have similar economic programmes but are divided by the past -- a large number of UW activists frowns on forming an alliance with the descendants of an authoritarian communist party.
Markets are generally unhappy with the ex-communist's current partners, the Polish Peasant Party (PSL), and would fear the broadly anti-liberal force extending its influence, they said.

"An SLD-lead coalition would be the best outcome for the markets. It would be preferable if it wasn't an SLD-PSL coalition, but, say, an SLD-Union for Freedom coalition," said Joseph Karazin, chief economist at Societe Generale in London.
"If the current coalition gets back in, especially with a bigger majority for the SLD, then there would be a big relief rally in the market," he added.
THE FLOOD FACTOR
The SLD's chances looked fairly good until recent severe flooding hit Poland -- people in stricken areas blamed the government for slow and inadequate help.

A poll earlier this week showed support might be growing for a coalition uniting the Solidarity Election Action (AWS) and the UW. The two sides share common roots in former anti-communist opposition, but often fight bitterly on issues ranging from abortion to the economy. Personal rivalries are a factor too.
The parties may yet be brought together and former president Lech Walesa, still wielding some influence on the right, is putting his weight behind the idea.
The poll showed support for a UW-Solidarity coalition was expressed by 20 percent of those polled by the PBS polling organisation compared with 12.4 percent for the existing coalition.
SLD PREFERENCE BASED ON RECORD

Economists said their preference for an SLD-led coalition was based mainly on investor familiarity with what is seen as the current government's positive approach to privatisation, foreign direct investment or budget deficit control.

"We favour the SLD purely on grounds of familiarity. All the parties are playing their cards very close to their chests so it is very difficult to have preferences," said Robert Beange, economist at Lehman Brothers in London.

The SLD-PSL coalition took power in 1993, inheriting from their centre-right predecessors a recovering economy. Since then, the dominating SLD, which groups many of the new business class, has kept the country firmly on the path of market reforms and integration with the West.

It managed to win the confidence of the markets even though some economists at home and abroad have complained about delays in privatisation and "networking" as well as relatively slow progress in fighting inflation.
"Clearly the SLD have done a pretty good job and everyone is happy with the direction they are going," said Andrew Kenningham, economist at Merrill Lynch in London.

Economists acknowledge that the AWS has vowed to favour fiscal tightening and issued statements calling on investors to "sleep at ease." But these encouraging words and the right-wing tag are not enough to win instant credibility.
"The AWS, although called right-wing, is not more pro-market than the ex-communist SLD," said Tony Norfield, chief economist at ABN Amro Bank in London.

The AWS groups some 30 right-wing parties ranging from pro-market liberals to Catholic traditionalists, populists and trades unionists. The diversity made the task of formulating policy arduous and fuels fears that the party may split up when it comes to making difficult policy choices.
Analysts said the AWS's stance on economic issues has often been unclear and it had yet to convince markets it could react to negative effects of the floods and growing current account deficit.
"There has been much talk about slower privatisation under the AWS which would clearly be not desirable," said Beange.
Economists said the AWS did not seem enthusiastic about foreign direct investment and may find it difficult to control wage growth because of its trade union core.

AWS leader Marian Krzaklewski has vowed to speed up privatisation so as to leave only 20 percent of national assets in the hands of the state against the current 50 percent, and to press ahead with returning property confiscated under communism.

He has also promised lower taxes -- highly unlikely now as the government must pay for the reconstruction of the flood-devastated southwest -- and a reform of the social security system. The AWS wants to use housing construction as the engine of growth and is committed to a strong, convertible zloty and low inflation.
Economists said these pledges could be tested only by a budget, due to be constructed after the election.

"Whoever gets in after September 21 will have to convince the markets that fiscal discipline is still a priority, especially given that there will be some slippage because of the flood," said Societe Generale's Karazin.
WEAK GOVERNMENT WOULD BE WORST SCENARIO

So far the ruling coalition wants a budget deficit of 1.9 percent of gross domestic product for next year against a 2.8 percent target for this year, while the central bank, the International Monetary Fund and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development say 1.5 percent is the upper limit.

While worried about the potential gains of the populist Movement for the Reconstruction of Poland, marching under patriotic and Christian slogans, and the unexpected popularity of the populist Pensioners Party, analysts said the worst scenario would put together the AWS and the PSL.
"The PSL has been a real pain in the neck sometimes and opposed the reforms...while the Solidarity groups are far more protectionist," said Merrill Lynch's Kenningham.
Some economists also said that no matter which group comes out victorious, be it SLD or AWS, it was important that they were able to build a clear majority.

"What I fear most is a weak coalition which is held hostage by the Peasant Party or the Pensioner's Party. The budget implications of that would be far worse than if we had a stable coalition, a stable government of either end of the spectrum," said Lehman Brother's Beange.
